newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada approves Arctic diamond mine.
newsitem.headline: Canada approves Arctic diamond mine.

text.p: The Canadian government gave final approval Friday to an C$860 million ($647 million) Arctic diamond mine proposed by Australia's Broken Hill Proprietary Co. Ltd. and Canada's Dia Met Minerals Ltd.
"This project has the full support of the government of Canada," said Ron Irwin, the federal minister responsible for the North.
"This diamond mining project is important to northerners and to all of Canada," he said at a ceremony in Yellowknife, the capital of the Northwest Territories.
The companies plan to build the mine at Lac de Gras, an isolated wilderness of lakes and tundra on the Arctic frontier. BHP has 51 percent of the project and Dia Met 29 percent.

The diamond mine would be Canada's first. It is expected to add C$6.2 billion ($4.7 billion) to Canada's gross domestic product over its projected 25-year life and create about 1,000 jobs during mine construction.
After the news, Dia Met's Class B stock climbed C$1.55 ($1.17) to C$21.80 ($16.39) in Toronto. BHP's American Depositary Receipts were up 25 cents to $27.125 on the New York Stock Exchange.

Jim Excell, BHP's manager for the project, told the ceremony that diamond mining was scheduled to start in 1998. Preliminary construction has already started and work is due to begin in earnest next summer, he said.
The flow of diamonds from Canada is expected to alter the world market for the gems.

Analysts projected the Lac de Gras mine will produce 8 percent to 12 percent of the world's rough diamonds by the turn of the century. A large part of its production will consist of the most valuable gem-quality stones.
BHP, which controls the project, has not yet decided whether to market the output through the fabled De Beers diamond cartel.

Canadian government approval was granted Friday only after BHP made progress in striking agreements with the government of the Northwest Territories and aboriginal groups. The accords cover the sharing of economic benefits and environmental monitoring and protection.
Investors had been eagerly awaiting the decision after Canada gave approval in principle in August for the mine. Since then BHP has been in intense negotiations and has sealed several accords.

In reviewing progress Friday, the government said an environmental accord had been developed and was undergoing final technical and legal review. Also, a framework understanding for setting aside protected land in the area has been drafted.
An economic benefit agreement has been signed with one aboriginal group and progress has been made toward agreements with three other aboriginal groups.
